Start working on Linear ticket eng-2364 by fetching its details and creating a dedicated git worktree.

## Steps

### 1. Validate input
- `eng-2364` should be a Linear ticket ID like `ENG-1271`. If missing or malformed, ask the user.

### 2. Fetch ticket details from Linear
- Use `mcp__linear-server__get_issue` with the issue ID `eng-2364`
- Extract: title, description, and `branchName` (Linear provides this)
- If the Linear tool is unavailable, ask the user for a branch name manually

### 3. Determine branch name
- Use the `branchName` field from Linear if available (it's already formatted correctly)
- Otherwise derive it: lowercase the ticket ID + hyphenated slug of the title
  - Example: `ENG-1271 Implement filter search` → `eng-1271-implement-filter-search`
  - Strip special characters, replace spaces with hyphens, truncate to ~60 chars

### 4. Create git worktree
Run these from the repo root (the main working directory, not an existing worktree):

```bash
# Fetch latest main so the worktree starts from up-to-date origin/main
git fetch origin main

# Check if branch already exists
git branch --list <branch-name>

# Check if worktree already exists
git worktree list | grep <branch-name>
```

- **If worktree already exists**: skip to step 5, just `cd` into `.claude/worktrees/<branch-name>`
- **If branch does NOT exist**: `git worktree add -b <branch-name> .claude/worktrees/<branch-name> origin/main`
- **If branch already exists but no worktree**: reset the branch to `origin/main` first, then add the worktree:
  ```bash
  git branch -f <branch-name> origin/main
  git worktree add .claude/worktrees/<branch-name> <branch-name>
  ```

### 5. Enter the worktree
**Do NOT use the `EnterWorktree` tool** — it always creates a brand-new worktree and will duplicate the one you just created.

Instead, use `cd` to switch into the worktree directory:
```bash
cd .claude/worktrees/<branch-name>
```

All subsequent commands should run from this path.

### 6. Install dependencies and set up the worktree
After entering the worktree, run the following to bootstrap the environment:

```bash
pnpm install
```

This is required because worktrees share git objects but each needs its own `node_modules`.

### 6b. Copy .env files from the main repo into the worktree
`.env` files are gitignored, so each worktree needs its own copies. After `pnpm install`, copy all `.env` files (excluding `.env.example` files) from the main repo root into the matching relative paths in the worktree.

The main repo root is the working directory you were in before entering the worktree (e.g. `/Users/trang.doan/Desktop/code/discourse-graph`).

Run:
```bash
# From the main repo root, find all .env files (not .env.example) and copy them into the worktree
find . -name ".env*" \
  -not -name ".env.example" \
  -not -path "./.git/*" \
  -not -path "./node_modules/*" \
  -not -path "./.claude/worktrees/*" \
  | while read f; do
      dest=".claude/worktrees/<branch-name>/$f"
      mkdir -p "$(dirname "$dest")"
      cp "$f" "$dest"
    done
```

Report which files were copied so the user can confirm.

The copied `OBSIDIAN_PLUGIN_PATH` points at the main checkout's vault. Step 7 replaces it
with the vault leased to this worktree.

### 6c. Link the shared `dg-*` skills into the worktree

Claude Code only loads skills from `.claude/skills`, but the repo's shared skills live in
`.agents/skills`. Without this step they never load in the worktree: they cannot trigger on
their own descriptions and have no slash command.

Run from the main repo root, substituting the worktree path:

```bash
WT=".claude/worktrees/<branch-name>"
MAIN="$PWD"
mkdir -p "$WT/.claude/skills"
for src in "$MAIN"/.agents/skills/dg-*/; do
  s=$(basename "$src")
  if [ -d "$WT/.agents/skills/$s" ]; then
    # Relative link, so the worktree uses its own branch's copy of the skill.
    ln -sfn "../../.agents/skills/$s" "$WT/.claude/skills/$s"
  else
    # Branch predates the skill; fall back to the main checkout's copy.
    ln -sfn "$MAIN/.agents/skills/$s" "$WT/.claude/skills/$s"
  fi
done
ls -l "$WT/.claude/skills/"
```

Verify each link resolves before moving on:

```bash
for d in "$WT"/.claude/skills/dg-*; do
  [ -f "$d/SKILL.md" ] || echo "BROKEN: $d"
done
```

These links are gitignored (`.claude/*`), so they are local to this machine and add nothing
to the diff. Use a glob rather than a variable list: zsh does not word-split unquoted
variables, so `for s in $SKILLS` silently iterates once with the whole string.

### 7. Ask the user which app to start
Ask the user which app they want to run in dev mode. Common options:
- **Roam**: `SUPABASE_USE_DB=none pnpm -C <worktree>/apps/roam dev`
- **Obsidian**: `node ~/.claude/skills/obsidian-vault/scripts/vault.mjs dev --worktree <worktree>`
  - This leases a free local-db vault and writes `OBSIDIAN_PLUGIN_PATH` and `SUPABASE_USE_DB` for
    it into `<worktree>/apps/obsidian/.env`. It then starts the watcher. A later plain `pnpm dev`
    and CDP runs use the same vault. Add `--db production` only if the user asks to test against
    prod (testVault123).
  - For **None**, still run `vault.mjs claim --worktree <worktree>` if the ticket touches
    apps/obsidian, so the `.env` doesn't keep pointing at the main checkout's vault.
  - **Exit 2** means every vault in that pool is taken. Follow the `obsidian-vault` skill: ask the
    user which vault to take over, then rerun with `--take <vault>`. Never pick one yourself.
  - On success, pass the printed `obsidian://open?path=` URL to the user, so they open that vault.
- **None**: just set up the environment without starting a dev server

If the user says Roam, also switch the Roam dev symlink:
```bash
ln -sfn <worktree>/apps/roam/dist ~/roam-ext-dev
```
and remind them to reload the developer extension in Roam.

Run the chosen dev command in the background so the user can continue working.

**Dev server gotchas** (learned the hard way — don't rediscover these):

- The filter flag is `--filter`, not `--F`. Turbo 2.5.6 rejects `--F=roam` outright.
- Prefer `pnpm -C <abs-path> <app> dev` over `turbo dev --filter=<app>`. `turbo dev --filter=roam`
  also runs the `@repo/database#dev` dependency, which requires Docker Desktop plus an explicit
  `SUPABASE_USE_DB`; if Docker isn't running turbo fails the *entire* run even though the app
  itself built fine. Going through `pnpm -C` skips the dependency graph.
- `SUPABASE_USE_DB` must be one of `local | branch | production | none | implicit`
  (see `packages/database/src/dbDotEnv.mjs`). Use `none` for work that doesn't touch the database.
- **Always bake the absolute worktree path into the command.** The Bash tool's cwd resets to the
  main repo between calls, so a backgrounded `pnpm --filter roam dev` with no path silently builds
  the *main repo's* `dist` — not the worktree the symlink points at. `pnpm -C <abs-path>` makes the
  path intrinsic to the command so it can't be dropped.
- After starting, verify before reporting success: confirm the log says `built with 0 errors` **and**
  that `<worktree>/apps/roam/dist` has a fresh mtime. A background task that failed still returns a
  task ID.

### 8. Ingest any saved session context
The branch may have been worked on before (e.g. reset from an existing branch).
Check for recorded session context:

```bash
bash ~/.claude/scripts/session-context.sh resolve
```

- If `CONTEXT_EXISTS=yes`, **read the `CONTEXT_FILE`** and load it as working context
  (`Next step`, `Open questions`, `Key decisions`, `Dead ends`).
- If `CONTEXT_EXISTS=no` or the command errors, continue — this is a fresh start.

### 9. Show context
After setup, display:
- Ticket ID and title
- Branch name you're on
- Brief description from the ticket (if available)
- Which app dev server is running (if any), and for Obsidian, which vault is leased
- That the shared `dg-*` skills are linked and resolving
- If prior session context was found: its `TL;DR` and `Next step`
- A short "ready to work" confirmation
- Remind the user they can run `/checkpoint` to save session context before wrapping up

content.text:
Clean up the git worktrees and local branches for a Linear ticket after work is done.

A ticket usually leaves behind more than one branch: the real branch plus `tmp-*`,
`rebase-test-*`, `pr-*`, `backup/*` and `snapshot-*` experiments. Find them all,
classify them by whether deleting is reversible, and let the user choose.

## Steps

### 1. Validate input
- `eng-2322` should be a Linear ticket ID like `ENG-1271`. If missing or malformed, ask the user.
- Normalize to lowercase and extract the bare number (`ENG-1271` → `eng-1271`, number `1271`).
- Accept a full branch name or a doubled prefix (`eng-eng2084`) and reduce it to the number.
  Only stop and ask if the number itself is ambiguous or absent.

### 2. Find everything related to the ticket
Match on the **number**, not the full branch name, across all three:

```bash
git fetch origin -q
git worktree list | grep -i <number>          # dir name OR branch name may match
git branch --list "*<number>*"
git branch -r --list "*<number>*"
```

Two traps that have bitten before, both worth an explicit check:

- **A worktree directory named for this ticket may be checked out on a different
  branch.** Always read the branch from `git worktree list`, never infer it from the
  directory name. If the branch belongs to another ticket, do not remove that
  worktree — check its PR state and report it instead.
- **A branch for this ticket may live in a directory named for another ticket.**
  So search worktrees by branch name too, not just by path.

If nothing matches at all, tell the user and stop.

### 3. Check each worktree for uncommitted work
```bash
git -C <worktree-path> status --short
```
- Dirty or untracked files: warn the user and ask whether to force-delete or abort.
- Exception: if every untracked file is 0 bytes, say so and proceed — there is nothing
  to lose. Verify with `wc -c`, don't assume from the name.
- Back up gitignored env files before removing, since worktree removal destroys them:
  ```bash
  find . -name ".env*" -not -path "*/node_modules/*"
  ```
  Copy them to the scratchpad and report the count.

### 4. Establish that deleting is safe
`git merge-base --is-ancestor <branch> origin/main` returns false for squash-merged
branches, so it proves nothing on its own. **Never delete on merge status alone.**

For each branch, determine whether its tip survives deletion — is it reachable from a
remote ref, or from a branch that is checked out in a worktree?

```bash
tip=$(git rev-parse "$b")
git for-each-ref --contains "$tip" --format='%(refname)' refs/remotes | head -1
```

- **Reachable** → safe, deletion is reversible.
- **Not reachable** → the local branch is the only copy. Deleting is permanent.

When a branch is ahead of a merged PR head, confirm the content actually landed rather
than trusting the commit count. Isolate its own contribution from main-drift:

```bash
BASE=$(git merge-base "$b" "$MERGED_HEAD")
git diff --stat "$BASE" "$b" -- <app-path>          # what the branch itself added
git log --format= --name-only "$BASE..$b" | sort -u  # files it touched
```

Then for each touched file, count lines the branch has that the merged side lacks
(`git diff "$b" origin/main -- "$f" | grep -c '^-[^-]'`). Zero across all touched files
means the work shipped. Also compare file *lists* — a file present at the branch tip and
absent from main is unshipped work, and is the case most worth surfacing.

Sanity-check the comparison itself before trusting a clean result: run it against an old
commit and confirm it returns a non-zero count. A silently broken loop that reports
"nothing unique everywhere" is the failure mode to guard against.

If the ticket merged into an integration branch rather than `main` (check the PR's
`baseRefName`), verify against that branch — `main` will give a misleading answer.

### 5. Present the findings and let the user select
Show a table of every worktree and branch found, with: branch, ahead/behind its remote,
PR state, and whether deletion is reversible. Group the experiments (`tmp-*`,
`rebase-test-*`, `pr-*`, `backup/*`, `snapshot-*`) separately from the real branch.

- Delete the reversible ones directly, naming them.
- For anything **not** reachable from a surviving ref, ask before deleting, grouped so
  the choice is quick. Never blanket-delete these.
- Leave alone unless explicitly chosen: branches with commits dated today, integration
  branches that live worktrees target, and tool-generated checkpoints (`entire/*`).

### 6. Remove
```bash
node ~/.claude/skills/obsidian-vault/scripts/vault.mjs release --worktree <worktree-path>  # stop its Obsidian watcher, free its vault
git worktree remove <worktree-path>        # --force only if the user confirmed
git branch -D <branch> [<branch> ...]
git worktree prune                          # clear registrations for vanished dirs
```
Run `git branch -D` from the main checkout, not from inside a worktree being removed.

### 7. Confirm
Report what was removed with its old SHA, what was kept and why, and — when the check in
step 4 turned up work that exists in no merged PR — say exactly where it now survives.

name: Main - Obsidian Beta Release
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
    paths:
      - "apps/obsidian/**"
      - "packages/database/**"
      - "packages/utils/**"

permissions:
  contents: write

concurrency:
  group: obsidian-beta-release
  cancel-in-progress: false

env:
  OBSIDIAN_PLUGIN_REPO_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.OBSIDIAN_PLUGIN_REPO_TOKEN }}
  PUBLISH_REPO: DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph-obsidian
  # Inlined into the bundle at build time by scripts/compile.ts. Without it the
  # plugin falls back to a dev URL, so released builds call localhost.
  NEXT_API_ROOT: https://discoursegraphs.com/api
  SUPABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.SUPABASE_URL }}
  SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY: ${{ secrets.SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY }}
  GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}

jobs:
  beta-release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout Code
        uses: actions/checkout@v6
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Install pnpm
        uses: pnpm/action-setup@v6
        with:
          version: 10.15.1
          run_install: false

      - name: Setup Node.js environment
        uses: actions/setup-node@v6
        with:
          node-version: "22"
          cache: "pnpm"

      - name: Install Dependencies
        run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

      - name: Compute next beta version
        id: version
        env:
          # Releases exist only in the publish repo, never in the monorepo, so the
          # lookup needs an explicit --repo and a token that can read that repo.
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ env.OBSIDIAN_PLUGIN_REPO_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          # manifest.json is the plugin's canonical version: it is what Obsidian
          # and the community store read. package.json is private and its version
          # is incidental.
          STABLE_VERSION=$(node -p "require('./apps/obsidian/manifest.json').version")
          LATEST_N=$(gh release list --repo "$PUBLISH_REPO" --limit 100 --json tagName --jq '.[].tagName' \
            | grep "^${STABLE_VERSION}-beta\." \
            | sed "s/^${STABLE_VERSION}-beta\.//" \
            | sort -n | tail -1)
          NEXT_BETA="${STABLE_VERSION}-beta.$(( ${LATEST_N:-0} + 1 ))"
          echo "Stable version: $STABLE_VERSION, next beta: $NEXT_BETA"
          echo "version=$NEXT_BETA" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Publish beta release
        run: cd apps/obsidian && npx tsx scripts/publish.ts --version ${{ steps.version.outputs.version }}

      - name: Sync Linear release
        uses: linear/linear-release-action@v0
        with:
          access_key: ${{ secrets.LINEAR_RELEASES_ACCESS_KEY_OBSIDIAN }}
          include_paths: "apps/obsidian/**,packages/database/**,packages/utils/**"

name: Stable Obsidian Release
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      version:
        description: "Stable version to release, e.g. 1.6.0. Must match an existing Linear release version."
        required: true
        type: string

permissions:
  contents: write

env:
  VERSION: ${{ inputs.version }}
  OBSIDIAN_PLUGIN_REPO_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.OBSIDIAN_PLUGIN_REPO_TOKEN }}
  # Inlined into the bundle at build time by scripts/compile.ts. Without it the
  # plugin falls back to a dev URL, so released builds call localhost.
  NEXT_API_ROOT: https://discoursegraphs.com/api
  SUPABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.SUPABASE_URL }}
  SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY: ${{ secrets.SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY }}

jobs:
  release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout Code
        uses: actions/checkout@v6
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Validate version input
        run: |
          if ! [[ "$VERSION" =~ ^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$ ]]; then
            echo "::error::Invalid version format: '$VERSION'. Expected semver like 1.6.0."
            exit 1
          fi

      - name: Install pnpm
        uses: pnpm/action-setup@v6
        with:
          version: 10.15.1
          run_install: false

      - name: Setup Node.js environment
        uses: actions/setup-node@v6
        with:
          node-version: "22"
          cache: "pnpm"

      - name: Install Dependencies
        run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

      - name: Publish stable release
        run: cd apps/obsidian && npx tsx scripts/publish.ts --version "$VERSION"

      # There is deliberately no version-bump commit here. The default-branch
      # ruleset requires a pull request and grants github-actions[bot] no bypass,
      # so a push from CI is always rejected on main. Bump apps/obsidian/
      # manifest.json and package.json in the release PR before dispatching.

      - name: Sync Linear release

663	}): Promise<void> => {

706

708	      () =>
709	        octokit.request("POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/releases", {

711	          repo,
712	          tag_name: tagName,
713	          name: releaseTitle,

716	        }),

718	    );

727

731	          ".json": "application/json",
732	          ".css": "text/css",

744	          octokit.request(`POST ${uploadUrl}`, {

747	              "content-length": String(stats.size),

753	      );

760	    }
761	  }
762	};

769	
770	  try {
771	    const isExternal = isExternalRelease(version);
772	    const releaseType = isExternal ? "external" : "internal";
773	    log(`Publishing Obsidian plugin v${version} (${releaseType} release)`);
774	
775	    await buildPlugin(obsidianDir);
776	
777	    if (fs.existsSync(tempDir)) {
778	      fs.rmSync(tempDir, { recursive: true });
779	    }
780	
781	    copyDirectory({ src: obsidianDir, dest: tempDir, baseDir: obsidianDir });
782	    copyBuildFiles(buildDir, tempDir);
783	    sanitizePackageJsonForMirror(tempDir, obsidianDir);
784	
785	    if (isExternal) {

792	    }
793	
794	    await createGithubRelease({
795	      version,
796	      releaseName,
797	    });

802	    throw error;
803	  } finally {
804	    if (fs.existsSync(tempDir)) {
805	      fs.rmSync(tempDir, { recursive: true });
806	    }
807	  }
808	};

812	    console.error(error);

You are working on the Obsidian plugin that implements the Discourse Graph protocol.

## Dependencies

Prefer existing dependencies from package.json.

## Obsidian Style Guide

Use the obsidian style guide from help.obsidian.md/style-guide and docs.obsidian.md/Developer+policies.

### Icons

Platform-native UI.
Lucide and custom Obsidian icons can be used alongside detailed elements to provide a visual representation of a feature.

Example: In the ribbon on the left, select Create new canvas ( lucide-layout-dashboard.svg > icon ) to create a canvas in the same folder as the active file.

Guidelines for icons

Store icons in the Attachments/icons folder.
Add the prefix lucide- before the Lucide icon name.
Add the prefix obsidian-icon- before the Obsidian icon name.
Example: The icon for creating a new canvas should be named lucide-layout-dashboard.

Use the SVG version of the icons available.
Icons should be 18 pixels in width, 18 pixels in height, and have a stroke width of 1.5. You can adjust these settings in the SVG data.
Adjusting size and stroke in an SVG.
Utilize the icon anchor in embedded images, to tweak the spacing around the icon so that it aligns neatly with the text in the vicinity.
Icons should be surrounded by parenthesis. ( lucide-cog.svg > icon )
Example: ( ![[lucide-cog.svg#icon]] )

### Function guides

- Any function that deals with querying vault's frontmatter, default to using Datacore API first, then write fallback where you use `plugin.app.vault.getMarkdownFiles()` to iterate through each file's frontmatter

## Plugin Store Guidelines

These rules must be followed for the plugin to be accepted into the Obsidian community plugin store.

### Security

- Never use `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, or `insertAdjacentHTML` with user-controlled content
- Use Obsidian DOM helpers instead: `createEl()`, `createDiv()`, `createSpan()`

### App instance

- Always use `this.app` — never the global `app` object

### Event listeners

- Register all event listeners via `this.registerEvent()` so they are automatically cleaned up on plugin unload

### UI text

- Use sentence case in settings headings and labels (not title case)
- Prefer `setHeading()` over raw HTML heading elements (`<h1>`, `<h2>`, etc.)

### Commands

- Do not set default hotkeys — they conflict with other plugins
- Use the correct callback type: `callback` for always-available commands, `checkCallback` when the command is conditionally available, or the editor variants for editor-scoped commands
- Do not manually prepend the plugin ID to command IDs — Obsidian adds it automatically

### Workspace

- Do not store references to custom views — look them up fresh each time they are needed
  Don't do this:
  `this.registerView(MY_VIEW_TYPE, () => this.view = new MyCustomView());`
  Do this instead:
  `this.registerView(MY_VIEW_TYPE, () => new MyCustomView());`
  To access the view from your plugin, use `Workspace.getActiveLeavesOfType():`

```
for (let leaf of app.workspace.getActiveLeavesOfType(MY_VIEW_TYPE)) {
  let view = leaf.view;
  if (view instanceof MyCustomView) {
    // ...
  }
}
```

- Do not detach leaves during plugin unload

### Editor

- Prefer the Editor API over `Vault.modify()` when the note is currently open in the editor
- Prefer `Vault.process()` instead of `Vault.modify()` to modify a file in the background

### Mobile compatibility

- Node.js and Electron APIs (`fs`, `crypto`, `os`) are unavailable on mobile
- If the plugin targets mobile, use web API equivalents: `SubtleCrypto` instead of `crypto`, `navigator.clipboard` for clipboard access
- Regex lookbehind assertions are not supported on some mobile — avoid them if possible

### Code quality

- Use `const`/`let` — never `var`
- Prefer `async`/`await` over `.then()` chains
- Minimize `console.log` — remove debug logs before shipping
- Do not hardcode styles inline — use CSS classes and Obsidian's CSS variables

## Unit tests

Vitest runs the plugin's pure logic in a Node environment: `pnpm test:unit` (or `pnpm test:watch` while working). The repository-wide `pnpm ci:validate` picks it up through the `test:unit` script.

- Put tests in `src/**/__tests__/<module>.test.ts`, next to the code they cover. Tests covering the test scaffolding itself live in `test/`; those two globs are the whole of `include` in `vitest.config.mts`.
- Import the module under test through the `~` alias, as the source does.
- `obsidian` ships type declarations with no runtime entry point, so `vitest.config.mts` aliases it to `test/obsidianStub.ts`. Add to that stub whatever a new test needs to load its module; use `vi.mock("obsidian")` in the test itself when the test needs to assert on a call.
- Obsidian's own objects are large. Build the slice the code path reads and cast it (`{ metadataCache: … } as unknown as App`) rather than constructing a whole `App` or `TFile`.
- Logic that needs a live vault, editor, or workspace is not covered here — extract the decision into a util and test that.

### Keeping the stub honest

The stub is hand-written, so it can be wrong about the API today and can fall behind when the `obsidian` dependency is bumped. Two mechanisms catch that. Each runs under exactly one command, so run `pnpm ci:validate` to get both.

`test/obsidianStub.conformance.ts` type-checks each stub member against the real declaration. It is type-only and matches none of the vitest globs, so only `pnpm check-types` enforces it. Keep it inside the `tsconfig.json` include, or the drift check disappears with no signal.

- Members with real behavior are fully conformant.
- Shells, which exist only so an importing module loads, are checked for the export name alone. When a shell gains behavior, move it to the conformant group.
- Every export must appear in one group or the other, so adding one without classifying it fails the build.

`test/obsidianStub.test.ts` pins the behavior the stub reimplements, which the type checker cannot see. It is type-checked like any other file, but only `pnpm test:unit` runs its assertions.

### Verifying the stub

Type declarations cannot tell you what a function returns for a given input, so do not guess it. Obsidian ships its implementation in `obsidian.asar`, in the resources directory of the installed app, and the current cases were settled by reading it. Two details it settled: `normalizePath("/")` returns `"/"`, and `TFolder.isRoot()` tests `path === "/"` rather than a null parent.

The bundle is minified, so it takes two steps: find the exported name to learn its minified name, then find that function. The example below is a macOS path; on Windows and Linux locate `obsidian.asar` under the install directory and substitute it.

```
node -e 'const s=require("fs").readFileSync("/Applications/Obsidian.app/Contents/Resources/obsidian.asar","utf8");
  const i=s.indexOf("normalizePath:()=>");
  console.log(s.slice(i, i+80));'
```

Read the behavior and reimplement it; do not paste the bundle's code into this repository. Pin whatever you learn in `obsidianStub.test.ts`, and name the test `diverges: …` when the stub deliberately does something else.

---
name: create-obsidian-release
description: Create a release for the Discourse Graphs Obsidian plugin from a requested semantic version. Use when asked to create or prepare an Obsidian plugin release.
---

Create a release for the Discourse Graphs Obsidian plugin with version $ARGUMENTS.

Follow these steps:

## 1. Validate input

- The argument should be a semver version number (e.g. `0.5.4`). If not provided or invalid, ask the user.

## 2. Find the previous release

- Run: `gh release list --repo DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph-obsidian --limit 5`
- Identify the most recent existing release (the one just before the new version being created).
- Note its tag name and published date.

## 3. Find Obsidian-related PRs since the last release

- Run: `gh pr list --repo DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph --state merged --limit 100 --json number,title,mergedAt,labels --jq '.[]'` and filter to PRs merged **after** the previous release date.
- For each PR, check which files it touches: `gh pr view <number> --repo DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph --json title,body,files`
- A PR is Obsidian-related if it touches files in `apps/obsidian/` or shared `packages/` used by Obsidian.
- Exclude PRs that only touch `apps/roam/`, CI workflows, or root dev tooling (prettier, eslint, husky configs) unless they meaningfully affect the Obsidian plugin.

## 4. Categorize the PRs

Group them into:

- **Features**: New functionality or meaningful enhancements
- **Bug Fixes**: Fixes to existing behavior
- **Internal**: Refactors, docs, dev tooling, plugin store compliance, README updates

## 5. Generate the changelog

Format it as:

```
# Changelog

## v{VERSION}

### Features

- **Short title**: Description ([#NNN](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/NNN))

### Bug Fixes

- **Short title**: Description ([#NNN](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/NNN))

### Internal

- **Short title**: Description ([#NNN](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/NNN))
```

Omit any section that has no entries.

## 6. Show the changelog to the user and ask for confirmation

Present the generated changelog and ask if they want to:

- Edit anything before publishing
- Proceed with creating/updating the release

## 7. Create or update the release

**Prerequisites:**

- `OBSIDIAN_PLUGIN_REPO_TOKEN` must be available — the script loads `apps/obsidian/.env` automatically via `dotenv`, so no manual `export` is needed as long as the token is in that file.

**Check if the release tag already exists:**

```
gh release view v{VERSION} --repo DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph-obsidian
```

**If the release does NOT exist** — run the publish script. This builds the plugin, uploads the release assets (`main.js`, `manifest.json`, `styles.css`), and creates the GitHub release:


content.text:
Yes, and it's the better source. The publish repo's `main/manifest.json` reads **`1.7.1`**, which matches the latest stable tag. It's public, and `updateMainBranch` rewrites it on every stable release, so it's always the version the community store is serving. Here's the plan built on that.

## Plan: ENG-2364 beta versioning

**Root cause:** the beta base comes from the monorepo's `apps/obsidian/manifest.json`. The stable workflow can't push a bump to main (the branch ruleset blocks `github-actions[bot]`), and `publish.ts`'s `updateLocalVersion` only changes the runner's throwaway checkout. So the base has been stuck at `1.5.2` through stable releases `1.6.0`, `1.7.0` and `1.7.1`.

**Fix** (`obsidian-main.yaml`, "Compute next beta version" step):
1. Read the stable version from the publish repo: `gh api repos/$PUBLISH_REPO/contents/manifest.json`. The step already uses `OBSIDIAN_PLUGIN_REPO_TOKEN`.
2. Base the beta on **stable + 1 patch**: `1.7.1` gives `1.7.2-beta.N`. In semver `1.7.1-beta.N` is *older* than `1.7.1`, so BRAT users on 1.7.1 would see those betas as downgrades. **This is my recommendation. Tell me if you'd rather keep `1.7.1-beta.N`.**
3. Number the betas per base, as the step does now. The first build after this change is `1.7.2-beta.1`, and the count starts over at `.1` after each stable release.
4. Update the step's comment, which wrongly says the monorepo `manifest.json` is canonical.

**Leave alone (out of scope):**
- `updateLocalVersion` in `publish.ts` writes to a checkout that's thrown away. It's dead in CI but harmless, and only matters for local runs.
- The stale `1.5.2` in the monorepo's `manifest.json`/`package.json` no longer affects betas. I'll mention it in the PR as a possible follow-up rather than fix it here.

**Verification:**
1. Run the new step's shell logic locally, with real `gh` data against the publish repo and `GITHUB_OUTPUT` pointed at a temp file. Expect `1.7.2-beta.1`.
2. Test the edge cases with fake tag lists:
   - existing `1.7.2-beta.3` gives `.4`
   - a new stable `1.8.0` gives `1.8.1-beta.1`
   - no betas yet gives `.1`
3. Lint the workflow with `actionlint`, if it's installed.
4. **No live dispatch.** Every run of this workflow publishes a real pre-release to the public publish repo. The first real check is the first merge to main after the PR lands, and I'll write that into the PR's testing notes.

Want me to go ahead with option 2's `1.7.2-beta.N` base?

The beta workflow now takes its base version from the live store version, and the live dispatch on this branch published **`1.7.1-beta.1`** as expected.

**Cause:** the workflow read the base version from this repo's `apps/obsidian/manifest.json`. CI isn't allowed to push the version bump to main after a stable release, so that file stayed at `1.5.2` through the `1.6.0`, `1.7.0` and `1.7.1` releases. That's why betas reached `1.5.2-beta.62`.

**Fix:** a single change in the "Compute next beta version" step of [obsidian-main.yaml](.github/workflows/obsidian-main.yaml):
- It now reads the version from `manifest.json` on the main branch of `discourse-graph-obsidian`. Every stable release rewrites that file, so it always matches what the community store serves.
- If that version isn't plain `x.y.z`, or the `gh api` call fails, the step stops instead of publishing a bad version.
- Betas are `1.7.1-beta.N`, as you chose. A one-line comment says this is deliberately below the stable version so automatic updates skip it.

**Verification:**
- **Local run against real data:** the extracted step returned `1.7.1-beta.1`.
- **Edge cases, all 7 passed (with a stand-in for `gh`):** a first beta after a release gets `.1`; beta numbers sort as numbers (`.10` after `.9`); a new stable release starts the count over; alpha tags and look-alikes such as `1.7.10-beta.N` are ignored; a malformed manifest or a failed API call stops the step.
- **Live run [37700529188](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/actions/runs/37700529188)** succeeded on every step. The new release is a pre-release with all three files, and its `manifest.json` says `1.7.1-beta.1`.
- **Publish repo main is unchanged:** it's still at `1.7.1`, last commit "Release v1.7.1" on Sep 30.
- **Formatting:** Prettier passes. I couldn't lint the workflow because `actionlint` isn't installed.

**Before you open the PR:**
- The workflow's "Sync Linear release" step also ran on this branch. It linked this branch's work to the in-progress Linear release, which would have happened at merge anyway.
- After a merge to main the next beta will be `1.7.1-beta.2`, because `.1` is now taken.
- This repo's `manifest.json` and `package.json` still say `1.5.2`. Nothing uses them for betas any more, and I left them alone as out of scope. The `updateLocalVersion` step in `publish.ts` only edits the CI runner's throwaway copy, so it's dead code in CI. Both could go in a follow-up ticket.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
name: Main - Obsidian Beta Release
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
    paths:
      - "apps/obsidian/**"
      - "packages/database/**"
      - "packages/utils/**"

permissions:
  contents: write

concurrency:
  group: obsidian-beta-release
  cancel-in-progress: false

env:
  OBSIDIAN_PLUGIN_REPO_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.OBSIDIAN_PLUGIN_REPO_TOKEN }}
  PUBLISH_REPO: DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph-obsidian
  # Inlined into the bundle at build time by scripts/compile.ts. Without it the
  # plugin falls back to a dev URL, so released builds call localhost.
  NEXT_API_ROOT: https://discoursegraphs.com/api
  SUPABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.SUPABASE_URL }}
  SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY: ${{ secrets.SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY }}
  GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}

jobs:
  beta-release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout Code
        uses: actions/checkout@v6
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Install pnpm
        uses: pnpm/action-setup@v6
        with:
          version: 10.15.1
          run_install: false

      - name: Setup Node.js environment
        uses: actions/setup-node@v6
        with:
          node-version: "22"
          cache: "pnpm"

      - name: Install Dependencies
        run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

      - name: Compute next beta version
        id: version
        env:
          # Releases exist only in the publish repo, never in the monorepo, so the
          # lookup needs an explicit --repo and a token that can read that repo.
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ env.OBSIDIAN_PLUGIN_REPO_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          # The publish repo's manifest.json is the live store version; CI can't push the
          # bump to this repo's main, so the local manifest.json goes stale after a release.
          STABLE_VERSION=$(gh api "repos/$PUBLISH_REPO/contents/manifest.json" --jq '.content' | base64 -d | jq -r '.version')
          if ! [[ "$STABLE_VERSION" =~ ^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$ ]]; then
            echo "::error::Unexpected stable version in $PUBLISH_REPO manifest.json: '$STABLE_VERSION'"
            exit 1
          fi
          LATEST_N=$(gh release list --repo "$PUBLISH_REPO" --limit 100 --json tagName --jq '.[].tagName' \
            | grep "^${STABLE_VERSION}-beta\." \
            | sed "s/^${STABLE_VERSION}-beta\.//" \
            | sort -n | tail -1)
          # Deliberately below the stable version in semver, so automatic updates never pick a beta.
          NEXT_BETA="${STABLE_VERSION}-beta.$(( ${LATEST_N:-0} + 1 ))"
          echo "Stable version: $STABLE_VERSION, next beta: $NEXT_BETA"
          echo "version=$NEXT_BETA" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Publish beta release
        run: cd apps/obsidian && npx tsx scripts/publish.ts --version ${{ steps.version.outputs.version }}

      - name: Sync Linear release
        uses: linear/linear-release-action@v0
        with:
          access_key: ${{ secrets.LINEAR_RELEASES_ACCESS_KEY_OBSIDIAN }}
          include_paths: "apps/obsidian/**,packages/database/**,packages/utils/**"

lines: +          # Separate command so bash -e (no pipefail) fails here instead of restarting at beta.1.

I opened PR [DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph#1530](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1530) against `main`. It's ready for review, not a draft.

<pr-created>https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1530</pr-created>

**A second commit, `47ae0c8e`, went in before the PR.** The fresh-context review found a latent bug. If `gh release list` failed, the error was hidden and the step restarted at `beta.1`. That tag now exists, so `publish.ts` would have skipped creating the release and the run would still have passed. The step now fetches the tags in a separate command, so a failure stops it. I re-ran all the edge cases plus a new "release list fails" case, and all 8 pass. Against real data the step now gives `1.7.1-beta.2`.

**All three review boxes in the PR body are unticked:**
- **Adherence check and full review:** a pre-PR hook only accepts a ticked box when the skill itself was invoked. My subagent applied the same checks without invoking `dg-pr-adherence-check` or `dg-delegated-full-review`, so each box has a one-line note saying what ran instead.
- **Scope check:** I compared the diff with "Done When" by hand, and nothing goes beyond it. I didn't run the `$scope-check` skill.
- **No Loom is recorded,** and the template asks for one on every PR.

If you want those boxes ticked, I can run the three skills on the current head and update the body.

**CI:** 1 check passing, 1 pending and 1 skipped, with no failures so far. I can turn on Auto-fix so CI failures get fixed automatically.

# Scope Check

Compare the completed change with its acceptance boundary. Return a copy-ready `Scope check` section unless the user requests the analysis too.

## Gather the Inputs

1. Resolve the Linear issue from an explicit `ENG-###` identifier, then from the PR or branch name. Fetch the issue with the Linear connector. If it is unavailable, ask for the ticket's `Problem`, `Solution`, and `Done When` sections.
2. Treat `Done When` as the acceptance boundary. Use `Problem` and `Solution` only to clarify that boundary, not to silently expand it.
3. Resolve the final change set from the supplied diff or PR. For a PR, inspect its metadata and complete diff. For the current branch, compare it with the PR base branch and include staged and unstaged changes.
4. Read linked decisions or ticket comments only when they explain an apparent scope expansion.

## Evaluate Scope

Map every material behavior or architectural change to a `Done When` criterion.

- Treat implementation details, tests, documentation, and generated files required to satisfy `Done When` as in scope.
- Flag broader abstractions, unrelated refactors, new dependencies, migrations, or support for cases not required by `Done When`.
- Do not treat a change as in scope only because it is useful or adjacent.

For each scope expansion, determine:

1. What broader abstraction or additional case was introduced?
2. Which current use case or ticket requires it, and why must it be included now rather than deferred?
3. Was anyone affected or consulted, and where is the discussion or decision recorded?

Do not invent missing justification. Mark it `Not documented` and recommend recording it in a Linear comment before the PR is merged.

## Format the Result

Use this form when the diff stays within scope:

```markdown
## Scope check

- [x] Ran `$scope-check` against ENG-#### and the final diff.
- Scope beyond `Done When`: None.
```

Use this form when the diff expands scope:

```markdown
## Scope check

- [x] Ran `$scope-check` against ENG-#### and the final diff.
- Scope beyond `Done When`: <what changed>
- Required now: <use case or ticket and why it cannot be deferred>
- Anyone affected or consulted: <Yes, No, or Not documented>
- Decision: <link to the discussion or decision, or `Not documented`>
```

If the ticket or diff cannot be resolved, leave the checkbox unchecked and state exactly what input is missing. Keep findings short and evidence-based.

Do not modify the issue, PR, or implementation unless the user explicitly asks.

# PR adherence check

Review the final change against the repository's current rules. Remain read-only unless the user authorizes fixes or PR updates. Do not post comments, request reviews, or change ticket status as part of this check.

## Resolve the evidence

1. Use the supplied PR or resolve the current branch's PR. Read its title, base and head commits, complete diff, body, checks, and review state. For local work, compare with the merge base of the intended PR base and include staged, unstaged, and relevant untracked files. Identify unavailable metadata and explicitly exclude unrelated local work.
2. Read root `AGENTS.md`, `STYLE_GUIDE.md`, `PR_GUIDELINES.md`, and `.github/pull_request_template.md`. Read nested `AGENTS.md` files applicable to every changed path. Resolve these from the target repository, not the skill's installation directory. If reviewing changes to the rules themselves, also inspect the base versions so removing a requirement cannot silently erase a finding.
3. Resolve the Linear ticket from an explicit identifier, then the PR or branch. Use the repository's `$scope-check` skill for the `Done When` boundary and its separate Scope check output. Missing ticket access or acceptance criteria blocks the scope conclusion, not independent standards checks.
4. Use command results and manual testing evidence tied to the reviewed revision. A checked box or successful unrelated CI job is not proof of all validation. Record the reviewed head and any local changes so stale evidence is identifiable.

## Evaluate adherence

- Inspect the complete diff and enough surrounding code to assess applicable TypeScript, UI, organization, comments, documentation, hygiene, and testing rules. Focus findings on introduced or modified code, not unrelated existing debt.
- Check title and branch conventions, ticket linkage, PR body requirements, size guidance, split justification, review entry points, testing evidence, Loom, and review/check status against `PR_GUIDELINES.md`.
- Distinguish mandatory rules from preferences. Words such as “prefer” and “ideally,” the 200-line target, and the five-file guideline need judgment. Above 400 changed lines, excluding tests, check for the required explanation and review guide rather than rejecting the size alone.
- Explain concerns briefly to the PR author so they can address them; formal rule citations and evidence for each finding are not required. Do not invent exceptions, team approval, testing outcomes, or video contents. If a required document is unavailable or rules conflict without a clear applicable resolution, report the gap instead of guessing.
- Respect workflow timing: missing Loom or review evidence can be reported as outstanding before requesting review while a draft is being prepared. Do not call future post-merge steps violations on an open PR.
- Keep scope expansions in Scope check. Verification is optional. Standards check only records whether the check ran.

## Return the result

Return a copy-ready section:

```markdown
## Standards check

- [x] Ran `$dg-pr-adherence-check` against the final diff and PR metadata.
```

The checkbox means the review ran, not that all requirements passed. If the diff cannot be resolved or the review could not run, leave it unchecked and tell the author what blocked it. Separately make any outstanding findings or unverified requirements known to the PR author so they can address them; do not require these details in the PR body. Rerun affected checks after changes to code, rules, or PR metadata.

# PR guidelines

This is the repository source for the DevOps PR process. Code standards live in [STYLE_GUIDE.md](STYLE_GUIDE.md); agent instructions live in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md). Production changes, releases, and work intake remain in DevOps.

## Scope and structure

- Use one PR per Linear ticket. You may batch very minor, unrelated changes of a few lines when they are low risk.
- Scope the ticket to one specific problem. If additional problems need attention, pause that additional work and check with the team or lead before implementing it.
- Use separate PRs for unrelated refactors, feature additions, dependency updates, and lint or style fixes. Keep scope to a single package or app when possible.
- For features spanning packages, make foundational changes such as types and shared utilities first, then use separate PRs for usage and integration.

## Size and review guidance

About 200 added plus removed lines is a useful target. Up to 400 lines is acceptable when the change is scoped and self-contained. Ideally, touch fewer than five files; repetitive mechanical changes can justify more. These are review guidelines, not automatic rejection thresholds.

Test changes do not count toward the 400-line threshold.

Above 400 changed lines, explain why the PR cannot reasonably be split. Include the main review entry points and intended testing path in Reviewer brief. Keep this concise rather than adding a file-by-file summary.

## Branches and PR metadata

- Use Linear's generated branch name through Copy Branch Name.
- For Linear-backed work, use `ENG-#### Exact Linear ticket title` as the PR title. This is the repository convention in place of the alternative title formats previously listed in DevOps.
- Start with [.github/pull_request_template.md](.github/pull_request_template.md). Treat the ticket as the source of truth rather than restating it. Follow the PR body guidance in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#pull-request-bodies).

## Before requesting review

- Run `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, then `pnpm ci:validate` from the repository root before opening a PR or declaring it ready. Resolve failures before requesting review. A draft must disclose unresolved validation blockers.
- Check applicable build and lint commands. Manually exercise changed behavior end-to-end, including relevant edge cases and alternative flows. Verification is optional; use it when checks and results help the reviewer.
- Read the complete final diff and review it against [STYLE_GUIDE.md](STYLE_GUIDE.md), including added and modified comments. Use inline PR comments for review-specific explanations and durable code comments for constraints future changes must preserve.
- Run `$scope-check` against the ENG ticket and final diff. Paste its Scope check section into the PR body. If `Done When` is missing, leave the checkbox unchecked and state that explicitly.
- Run `$dg-pr-adherence-check` against the final diff and PR metadata. Check the Standards check box when it has run. Make any outstanding findings or unverified requirements known to the PR author so they can address them.
- Complete the Local delegated full review required by the template, using `$dg-delegated-full-review` when no other full-review workflow is available.
- Include a Loom video for every PR, including backend, refactor, and infrastructure changes. Keep it under 2–3 minutes, show before/after for bug fixes, and narrate key decisions. Put the link in Loom video.
- Assign a reviewer when ready. Do not mark a draft ready while required evidence or reviews remain incomplete.

## After merge

Delete the PR branch after a successful merge. Creating a draft does not authorize merging or deleting branches.

content.text:
I ran all three checks on head `47ae0c8e`. They all passed, and the three boxes are now ticked in the body of [DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph#1530](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1530).

- **`$scope-check`:** nothing goes beyond "workflow is fixed and tested". The one changed step reads the stable version from the publish repo, rejects a malformed one, and stops when the release list can't be read. That last guard counts as part of the fix: with the new version source, `beta.1` already exists after every stable release.
- **`$dg-pr-adherence-check`:**
  - The title matches the ticket exactly, the branch is Linear's name, and the PR is one file and about 16 lines.
  - Each new comment explains a constraint a maintainer would otherwise get wrong.
  - CI's `validate`, `lint-changed-files` and `format-changed-files` pass.
  - `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile && pnpm ci:validate` passes locally on `47ae0c8e` with nothing cached; I added this to the Verification section.
- **`$dg-delegated-full-review`:** a fresh subagent found nothing. It followed the review instructions itself instead of calling `/code-review`, because that command can spawn more agents. It confirmed that only stable releases ever write the publish repo's `manifest.json`, so a beta can never become the base for the next beta.

**Still outstanding: the Loom.** The guidelines require one for every PR, infrastructure changes included, so the Loom section has no link yet. Record it before you assign a reviewer.

**Suggested CLAUDE.md addition:** "Run the three PR checks before `/create-pr`, and write the PR body file in a separate step from `gh pr create`." The pre-PR hook blocked creation twice: once because the skills hadn't been invoked, and once because it checked the body file before an edit in the same command had run. Want me to add it?
